title: Wellman Braud brings him to Duke Ellington's Cotton Club band
summary: Wellman Braud recommended him to Ellington, who was starting at the Cotton Club for about $72 a week; the Nest boss offered his job back if it failed, and Bigard joined Duke in late 1927.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Well, anyway, that came on, and then I met Wellman Braud from New Orleans, but I didn't know him in New Orleans because he had been in New York practically -- oh, years before I ever got there. But he heard about me and all that, so he came around and him and I got to be real good friends. And he was working with Duke at the Cotton Club. Duke had just gotten a job at the Cotton Club and he was looking for a
clarinet player, a saxophone player, and Braud told him about me. So he told Braud to bring me over to his apartment. He wanted to see me.

So I went over there and his job was paying, at that time, was $72 or something a week. That's about all it was. But it was a big band, a ten-piece band at the time. So I went over to him and he acted like he was not so interested or nothing, you know, so Braud was telling me -- he used to call me "Millet" -- he said, "Millet, take it," he said, "I think it's going to be good because you can do a lot of recording and you can play different things and all that." He said, "If you don't like it, then you can quit."

So I gave my notice at the Nest. So the boss was telling me, "Why you want to leave?" He said, "You make more money here than going over there. I know what you're going to get over there." I said, "Yeah, but it's a -- I've got a good opportunity to make some more money, a bigger band," and all that. So they said, "Well, tell you what." They said, "If you don't like it, your job is always open for you here," so that gave me more courage to go anyhow. And I went and I joined Duke.
'27, the latter part of '27. And then I -- well, I'll continue that a little later on.
